analysis.one_liner: Requires rent-to-own stores to disclose the full cost to own and gives customers new rights.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 16 cosponsors to set federal disclosure rules for rent-to-own stores was never taken up by the Senate Banking Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set the first federal rules for rent-to-own deals, where customers pay weekly or monthly to eventually own furniture, appliances, and electronics. Stores would have to state, in writing and on price tags and ads, the cash price, the total cost to own, and the number of payments, and customers would get rights like reinstating a contract after a missed payment. But the bill would also have overridden state laws that treat rent-to-own deals as credit and require stores to show an annual percentage rate, which is what the industry had long sought.
analysis.who_benefits: Rent-to-own customers — the bill's own findings say about 2.3 million households a year enter these transactions, and they are typically lower-income families buying furniture and appliances. They would get a standard, plainly-worded disclosure of the cash price, the total amount they'd pay to own the item, and every fee, plus the right to reinstate a contract after a missed payment, a limit of one late fee per missed payment, and bans on confessions of judgment, wage assignments, and waiving legal claims. State attorneys general would gain a new tool to sue abusive stores, and willful false disclosure would become a crime. Rent-to-own merchants would also gain something: a uniform federal rule that overrides state laws requiring annual-percentage-rate disclosure or treating the deals as credit.

how_it_helps.text: Stores would have to disclose, in writing before signing, the cash price of the item, the total cost to acquire ownership, the number of payments, and every fee or penalty separately — so a customer could see in one place that a TV renting for $20 a week might cost several times its cash price to own.
Price tags at the store and any advertising that mentions a payment amount would have to show the total rental-purchase cost and the number of payments needed to own the item.

Customers who miss a payment would get a defined window to reinstate the contract without losing their rights or prior payments, and could return the item at any time without owing charges beyond those already due.

The bill bans contracts from containing confessions of judgment, wage assignments, waivers of legal claims, or entry into a customer's home without consent, limits customers to one late fee per missed payment, and caps what a customer owes if rented property is lost or destroyed.
The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules, and a willful, knowing false disclosure would carry criminal penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own store chains would bear the cost: new disclosure forms, point-of-rental tags, advertising changes, reinstatement obligations, and exposure to FTC and state-AG enforcement plus civil suits and criminal penalties for willful violations. Companies that buy or take assignment of rental-purchase contracts would face liability when a violation is apparent on the face of the agreement. Merchants would gain in exchange a federal shield from state APR-disclosure and credit-characterization laws.

drawbacks.text: The bill would supersede any state law that regulates rent-to-own deals as a form of credit or requires disclosure of a percentage rate such as an annual percentage rate — so in states with tougher rules, customers could lose the very disclosure that lets them compare rent-to-own costs against borrowing the money instead.

It would shield companies that acquire rental-purchase contracts: they could be sued only if the violation is apparent on the face of the agreement, and a customer's signed acknowledgment of receiving disclosures would count as conclusive proof the disclosure was actually made.
The bill mandates disclosure but sets no ceiling on what stores can charge — the gap between the cash price and the total cost to own would remain entirely legal, as long as it is disclosed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For rent-to-own customers, the disclosure, reinstatement, and fee-limit provisions are real, concrete gains. But the bill was built on the framework the industry itself had long promoted: a federal floor that overrides state laws treating the deals as credit or requiring rate disclosure, plus narrow liability for companies that buy the contracts. A customer in a state with strong rent-to-own laws could come out worse off than before. On balance it trades standardized, honest paperwork for a weaker legal backdrop in stricter states, and it would not have lowered the price of renting to own by a dollar.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee from May 2011 until the Congress ended in January 2013, never getting a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action.

narrative.text: Senator Mary Landrieu introduced the bill on May 4, 2011, joined by Senators Roger Wicker and Roy Blunt, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
Sixteen senators cosponsored it — 12 Republicans and 4 Democrats — giving it bipartisan backing.
That referral was the bill's only action; the committee never reported it, no vote was ever held, and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own merchants: they avoided new federal disclosure and reinstatement mandates and their compliance costs, while customers got nothing and the federal preemption the industry wanted never arrived either — state rules simply stayed as they were.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 12 of 47 Senate Republicans and 4 of 51 Senate Democrats cosponsored — but no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would impose real obligations on the industry — standardized cost disclosures, reinstatement rights for customers, and penalty exposure — but it would also lock in the industry's core legal position by overriding state laws that treat rental-purchase deals as credit and requiring stores to show only flat totals, never an annual percentage rate. Customers would see clearer paperwork; they would still not see the deal framed as an interest rate they could comparison-shop.

industries.industry: Purchasers of rental-purchase contracts (assignees and finance companies)
industries.note: The bill would let customers sue these companies only when a violation is apparent on the face of the agreement, and would treat a customer's signed acknowledgment of disclosures as conclusive proof they were made. That narrows liability for the companies that buy these contracts, at the expense of customers' ability to recover.
